prompt: Which of these is a service level indicator in the sense of this lesson?
hint: A ratio of events customers feel.

choices.text: Average CPU of the API's tasks
choices.why: Easy to measure, and nobody leaves a shop over it.

choices.text: Requests without a 5xx over all requests
choices.why: Right. Good events over valid events, as customers see them.

choices.text: The number of tasks running
choices.why: A capacity figure, not a ratio of good events.

choices.text: Deployments per week
choices.why: A delivery measure, not what customers experience.

prompt: Health checks are counted as valid requests in the availability SLI. What happens to the number?

choices.text: It drops, because health checks fail often
choices.why: They succeed nearly always; that is the problem.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because they are filtered by AWS
choices.why: Nothing filters them unless the definition does.

choices.text: It becomes impossible to compute
choices.why: It computes fine; it just measures the wrong thing.

choices.text: It looks better than customers experience
choices.why: Right. Easy successes pad both sides of the ratio.

prompt: Why measure availability at the load balancer rather than inside the API's code?
hint: Think of a task that is down.

choices.text: A dead task's requests fail where the code never runs
choices.why: Right. The load balancer sees the 502; the API sees nothing.

choices.text: The load balancer's metrics are cheaper
choices.why: They are free, but cost is not why.

choices.text: The API's code cannot count requests
choices.why: It can count the ones it receives; the problem is the others.

choices.text: The load balancer excludes 4xx automatically
choices.why: It counts 4xx and 5xx separately; the definition decides.

prompt: At 99.9% over 30 days, how many minutes of total outage does the error budget allow?
At 99.5% over 30 days, with 1,000 requests a minute, how many requests may fail?
The budget for the month is spent on the 18th. What does an agreed budget policy say happens next?
hint: The policy was written before it was needed.

choices.text: The objective is lowered for the rest of the month
choices.why: Moving the target when it is missed makes it meaningless.

choices.text: Nothing, until the next month resets it
choices.why: A rolling window does not reset, and a policy nobody acts on is a dashboard.

choices.text: Reliability work first, risky changes wait
choices.why: Right. The number decides, without a debate.

choices.text: The team that caused it is replaced on call
choices.why: A budget policy is about priorities, not blame.

prompt: A team proposes 99.99% for a service whose customers never complained at 99.9%. What is the strongest objection?
hint: Each nine divides the budget by ten.

choices.text: CloudWatch cannot measure four nines
choices.why: Ratios of counts are measurable at any precision.

choices.text: 4.3 minutes a month: one bad deploy spends it all
choices.why: Right. The budget becomes too small to ship with, for no customer benefit.

choices.text: A higher objective costs more in CloudWatch
choices.why: The metrics cost the same; the cost is in engineering and freedom to change.

choices.text: Objectives above 99.9% are not allowed by AWS
choices.why: The objective is the team's promise; AWS does not limit it.

prompt: The SLO is 99.9%. Over the last hour, 0.6% of requests failed. What is the burn rate?
hint: Error rate divided by the budget rate.

prompt: Why does a burn-rate alert check a short window as well as the long one?

choices.text: So it stops paging once the problem is over
choices.why: Right. The hour stays bad after recovery; five minutes do not.

choices.text: The short window is cheaper to query
choices.why: Cost is not the reason; paging after recovery is.

choices.text: To page sooner on any single bad minute
choices.why: Both windows must burn; one bad minute alone does not page.

choices.text: Because CloudWatch keeps one-hour data only 15 days
choices.why: Hourly data is kept 15 months; retention is unrelated.

prompt: In the `recovered` scenario, why did `burn.py` print `no page`?

choices.text: The hour burned below 14.4
choices.why: The hour burned at 21.4, the same as the ongoing case.

choices.text: moto stopped returning data after 20 minutes
choices.why: Both windows returned their counts.

choices.text: The errors were 4xx, not 5xx
choices.why: The program counts the Errors metric; both scenarios had the same kind.

choices.text: The last five minutes burned at 1.0
choices.why: Right. Both must exceed 14.4, and the short one was back to normal.

prompt: A burn rate of 14.4 sustained for one hour spends ___% of a 30-day error budget.
Why is a rolling 30-day SLI on CloudWatch computed from five-minute sums rather than one-minute ones?

choices.text: Five-minute sums are more accurate
choices.why: A sum is exact at any period; the issue is age.

choices.text: One-minute data is kept 15 days
choices.why: Right. Five-minute data lasts 63, enough for a 30-day window.

choices.text: Metric math rejects one-minute periods
choices.why: It accepts them; the old data simply is not there.

choices.text: Five-minute queries are free
choices.why: GetMetricData is billed per metric requested, whatever the period.

prompt: In the metric math query, what does `"ReturnData": false` on the two sums do?

choices.text: Discards the data points from CloudWatch
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the query only shapes the answer.

choices.text: Makes them cheaper by skipping them
choices.why: They are still read and billed; only the answer omits them.

choices.text: Leaves them out of the answer
choices.why: Right. They feed the expression, which is the one returned.

choices.text: Turns them into alarms
choices.why: Alarms are separate; this is a query.

prompt: Put the steps of putting an SLO on the shop's API in order.
items: Define good and valid events at the load balancer
Choose the objective and the 30-day window
Write the budget policy and get it agreed
Add burn-rate alerts on two windows
trap: Alerts before the objective is the slip: a burn rate needs a budget to burn.

prompt: Match each burn rate, sustained, to how long a 30-day budget lasts.
hint: Thirty days divided by the rate.
